approachQuestion.prompt:
Priority dispatch. A read-only array contains n records in arrival order. Return a permutation of their original indices in ascending priority order, preserving arrival order among equal priorities. Each record has an opaque fixed-size priority key and payload reference. Keys support only a constant-cost order/equality comparator: no arithmetic, hashing, digit inspection, or bounded-domain indexing is available. There are 1 <= n <= 200,000 records. The result is an n-slot mutable integer array of original indices, not copied records. You may fill and rearrange that result during construction. Allocate n slots in proportional time; compare and swap indices in constant time, accessing their input priorities directly. Minimize deterministic worst-case comparison-model time, then peak auxiliary space. Input records must remain unchanged.

Example 1: Input priorities in arrival order: [2,1,2]. Output: [1,0,2].
Example 2: Input priorities in arrival order: [4,4]. Output: [0,1].

options.text: Initialize result with indices 0..n-1 and heapsort it iteratively by (priority at that index, index), using index as the tie breaker and no separate heap array.
options.feedback: Each original index uniquely breaks priority ties in arrival order. The result array itself holds the heap, and iterative sifting needs only a few variables.

options.text: Initialize result with original indices and perform stable iterative merge passes by priority, using a separate n-slot scratch array and left-first ties.
options.feedback: This produces the same stable index order with optimal worst-case time, but its scratch array is avoidable because iterative heapsort can use the permitted result workspace.

options.text: Initialize result with indices and stably insertion-sort them by priority.
options.feedback: The ordering is correct, but decreasing distinct priorities force repeated long shifts through sorted prefixes. A guaranteed faster comparison sort is available using the same output workspace.

options.text: Heapsort the output indices using priority alone, allowing equal keys to appear in either order.
options.feedback: Arrival order is required on ties. For priorities=[4,4], the permitted arbitrary tie order [1,0] violates the required result [0,1].

feedback.reason: Required output can provide mutable workspace, and original indices can enforce stable order even with an unstable sorting mechanism.
details: Allocate result and fill it with 0..n-1. Compare two stored indices by their input priorities, then by the indices themselves on a tie. Build a max heap in result using bottom-up iterative sift-down. Repeatedly swap the root with the last heap element, shrink the heap, and sift the root down iteratively. Return result. Use no separate heap, recursive calls, decorated entries, or payload copies.

Comparing original indices after equal priorities makes arrival order part of the total ordering. The heap itself need not be a stable sorting algorithm because that tie-breaker distinguishes records. Sifting inside the returned index array avoids a separate heap or copied payload records.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze heap-sort-output-indices, not the merge-sort alternative. What are worst-case time and peak auxiliary space in terms of n, including n=1? Count allocation/initialization, heap construction and all extraction/sift steps. The n-slot result is required output throughout construction and is excluded; the read-only records are input.
constraints: Choose the tightest standard bound for the complete execution. Count peak simultaneously live auxiliary storage; exclude supplied input and required output.
Word arithmetic, indexing, and copying one fixed-size element take constant time. No hashing or recursion is used.

options.text: O(n log(n + 1)) time, O(1) auxiliary space
O(n log(n + 1)) time, O(n) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Sort n output indices with iterative heap operations and constant helper storage.
details: Initialization and bottom-up heap construction cost O(n). Up to n extractions each require at most logarithmic sift work, giving tight worst-case O(n log(n+1)) total, including setup at n=1. The heap occupies the required result itself. Iterative sifting uses only counters, indices and temporary words, so auxiliary space is O(1). Tie comparisons use input priorities and the original index without allocating decorations or copying payloads.
“O(n log(n + 1)) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: The scratch array belongs to the partial merge-sort alternative. The analyzed heap is stored directly in the required result.
“O(n) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Heap construction is linear, but extracting and restoring heap order repeatedly adds logarithmic work per extraction in the worst case.
“O(n²) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: This is a loose upper bound; sift-down follows one heap path instead of shifting through a full growing prefix.
